title: Find the Peaks
statement: Given the array `mountain`, collect the index of every peak and return those indices in any order. An index counts as a peak when its value is strictly larger than the values on both its left and its right. Index `0` and the last index are never peaks. Return an empty list when no peak exists.
notes:
## Intuition

A peak depends only on its two neighbours, so a single pass that looks one step back and one step forward finds them all. The ends are skipped because they lack a neighbour on one side. This is a direct enumeration: every interior index is checked exactly once.

## Approach

1. Start with an empty list `peaks`.
2. Loop `i` over the interior indices, from `1` to `mountain.length - 2`.
3. Read the neighbours `left = mountain[i - 1]` and `right = mountain[i + 1]`.
4. If `mountain[i]` is strictly greater than both, append `i` to `peaks`.
5. Return `peaks` (it is already in increasing order, which is one of the accepted orders).

## Example 1, step by step

`mountain = [2, 4, 4]`. The only interior index is `i = 1` with `left = 2` and `right = 4`. `4 > 2` holds but `4 > 4` does not, so nothing is added and the answer is `[]`.

For `[1, 4, 3, 8, 5]` the checks give: `i = 1` (4 beats 1 and 3, peak), `i = 2` (3 loses to 4), `i = 3` (8 beats 3 and 5, peak), so the answer is `[1, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each interior index is compared with two neighbours.
- Space: O(1) besides the returned list.

## Pitfalls

- Use strict `>` on both sides; a plateau such as `[4, 4]` has no peak.
- Never report index `0` or the last index, even if they are the largest values.
- Stop the loop at `mountain.length - 2` so `mountain[i + 1]` stays inside the array.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `peaks` | indices found so far |
| `i` | the interior index being checked |
| `left`, `right` | the heights just before and just after `i` |

narration.3: Only interior indices can be peaks, so skip the first and the last.
narration.4: Height of the neighbour on the left.
narration.5: Height of the neighbour on the right.
narration.6: A peak must be strictly higher than both neighbours.
narration.7: Record this index as a peak.
narration.10: Return every peak found, in increasing index order.
